newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--More good news, what else?.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--More good news, what else?.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries, already buoyed by weak May U.S. retail sales, are awaiting further good news from the wholesale inflation front and a confirmation the Federal Reserve is on hold for the near term, market watchers said.
"People were not really long going into the retail sales," said one trader who commented on the 0.1-percent May drop.
"If we get another confirmation from the fundamentals that the Fed does not need to move, it's going to be party time again," he added.

Party time for bonds may be 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Friday with the release of the May Producer Price Index. The consensus forecast in a Reuters survey sees a mere 0.1-percent rise in both the PPI and the core PPI, ex-food and ex-energy.

"This would confirm the prevalent market view that the Fed is on hold in July," added the trader who pointed out the two-year Treasury note is yielding 6.06 percent and pricing no tightening for the foreseeable future.
The trader also expected U.S. Treasuries to further benefit from capital flows out of Europe where uncertainty about the single currency is enervating investors.
MCM MoneyWatch senior economist Astrid Adolfson confirmed the trader's comments regarding market expectations for Fed policy in July.

Adolfson said the latest poll of money managers conducted by her firm this week showed that only 5.0 percent of the respondents expected a U.S. rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next meets on July 1-2.

"And that was before the retail sales report," Adolfson stressed. "Just a week earlier, before the May employment report, 60 percent of the money managers we polled were expecting a Fed tightening in July."
The Fed, expecting an economic slowdown from the torrid pace of growth of the first quarter, has kept the federal funds rate at 5.50 percent since March 25.

"As long as there is no sign of inflation and Mr. (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan does not tighten, the party will go on forever," predicted Adolfson, noting that the Dow Jones industrial average vaulted above the 7700-level on Thursday for another record closing high.
"Definitely, it's uncharted territory," she added, noting the Fed no longer mentions "irrational exuberance" -- Greenspan's words of caution about asset prices in December.

"The market is happy, Mr. Greenspan is happy, the economy is fine, business and consumer confidence are okay," said Adolfson, describing the picture-perfect U.S. economic and financial market situation.

The rally into U.S. financial assets is accompanied -- and reinforced -- by a surging dollar reflecting global investors' hopes for U.S. capital gains compounded by hefty foreign exchange-related returns.
Tom Benfer, director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal, agreed that "portfolio managers are putting the money to work because the Fed is not going to move in July."

"European investors have to come to the United States which offers a vibrant economy versus stagnation in Europe and uncertainty about the European Monetary Union," said Benfer who expected further moves into U.S. assets.

With so much riding on expectation of an inflation-free U.S. expansion, the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment preliminary reading for June may provide one reason for caution. The index, set to be released to paying subscribers shortly before 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, has been steadily setting record highs.
